deep.reconstruction:
PART A (end of the argument begun on p.86 about 'Maurer's theorem'). Context from the previous page: Hilbert cites his own review of L. Maurer (Jahrbuch über die Fortschritte der Mathematik, Bd. 20, S. 102; Maurer, 'Über allgemeinere Invarianten-Systeme', Münch. Ber. 1888). In that review, Maurer's theorem says that the linear substitutions leaving a form invariant can be written with coefficients that are rational functions of parameters. Hilbert generalizes it to the linear self-transformations of an arbitrary algebraic variety. He shows it implies that a one-dimensional algebraic curve admitting a continuous group of self-transformations is rational. Then he sketches the converse.

The converse, as continued on this page:
(i) Restrict the group G by singling out ('ausschalten') the transformations that send certain points to themselves or to other prescribed points.
(ii) Do this so that the singled-out family is a one-parameter family under which some one-dimensional algebraic curve (an orbit closure) goes into itself.
(iii) By the curve theorem that curve is rational. So that one-parameter family can be parametrized rationally.
(iv) Single out further one-parameter families in the same way. Continue until the most general element of G is a composition g = g_1(t_1) g_2(t_2) ... g_r(t_r) of these one-parameter pieces.
(v) A product of rationally parametrized factors is rationally parametrized. This gives the generalized Maurer theorem.

Final remark: the theorem extends to the simultaneous invariance group of two forms F, G by applying it to the product F*G.

In modern terms, the scheme shows that a connected linear algebraic group is generated by one-parameter subgroups whose orbit closures are rational curves. Hence the group is unirational, i.e. it has a dominant rational parametrization. The argument is a heuristic sketch.

PART B (new topic). Let L(y) = 0 be a linear ODE of third order in x, with fundamental system y1, y2, y3. Consider

D(x;u) = det [[y1, y1', u1], [y2, y2', u2], [y3, y3', u3]] = 0.

Expanding along the last column (my expansion):
u1 (y2 y3' - y3 y2') - u2 (y1 y3' - y3 y1') + u3 (y1 y2' - y2 y1') = 0.

Geometric meaning (mine): if (u1:u2:u3) are point coordinates in P^2, D = 0 says u is collinear with y(x) = (y1:y2:y3) and y'(x). So u lies on the tangent line at the point with parameter x of the integral curve x -> (y1(x):y2(x):y3(x)). The equation is homogeneous in u, so it depends only on u1/u2 and u3/u2.

The next page continues: by inversion one gets x as a (generally multivalued) function of u1/u2 and u3/u2. This is the parameter of a tangency point of a tangent through u. Local solvability needs dD/dx = det[y, y'', u] to be nonzero (mine).

If monodromy acts by y -> A y, then D_{Ay}(x;u) = det A * D_y(x; A^{-1} u). So the function x(u) is invariant under the projective transformations u -> A u for A in the monodromy group of the ODE. This is a two-variable analogue of Schwarz–Poincaré inversion of y1/y2 for second-order equations. Hilbert compares it with Picard's functions of two variables (hyperfuchsian functions).
errors: Product trick for two forms: invariance of F*G does not imply invariance of F and G separately. Scalars can be traded (F -> cF, G -> G/c), and for equal degrees F and G can be swapped. So the stabilizer of F*G is in general larger than the simultaneous stabilizer, and one needs an extra step: take the connected component, normalize scalars, or intersect with the subgroup fixing each irreducible factor. This step is unstated.

The converse argument (one-parameter families whose orbits are curves, composed until the whole group is obtained) is only sketched. Why such one-parameter families exist and generate G, and why their orbit closures are algebraic curves, is assumed rather than shown.

What the argument yields is a rational parametrization by a dominant (generally not birational) map, i.e. unirationality. That matches the wording 'coefficients rational functions of parameters', but it is weaker than rationality of the group variety.
Part B: 'inversion' tacitly requires det[y, y'', u] to be nonzero and gives a multivalued x(u) (several tangents through a general point). The page does not discuss this.

results.what: Linear stabilizer groups of forms and of algebraic varieties admit parametrizations with coefficients rational in the parameters; the converse is obtained via one-parameter subgroups and the rationality of curves with a continuous automorphism group.
results.modern_name: Unirationality (rationality) of connected linear algebraic groups; generation by one-parameter subgroups; curves with infinite automorphism group (genus 0 case) are rational
results.usually_credited_to: L. Maurer (1888, 1894) for the original claim; rationality of connected linear algebraic groups in char 0 via Chevalley/Borel (1950s)

results.what: Extension to two forms by passing to their product
results.modern_name: Stabilizer of a product form (contains the simultaneous stabilizer)

results.what: For a 3rd-order linear ODE, det[y, y', u] = 0 (tangent lines of the integral curve) inverted to give x as a function of u1/u2, u3/u2, invariant under the monodromy group acting projectively
results.modern_name: Generalized Schwarz map / inversion of linear ODE (projective curve of solutions, dual curve); two-variable automorphic functions
results.usually_credited_to: Schwarz, Fuchs, Poincaré for order 2; Halphen, Picard (hyperfuchsian functions, 1880s) for analogues

deep.surprise_reason: These are notebook remarks extending a theorem Hilbert himself reviewed (Maurer 1888) plus a standard inversion idea à la Poincaré/Picard. The reduction to one-parameter subgroups and rational curves is a nice early sketch, but it is heuristic and close to Maurer's own ideas.

checkable.sympy: x,u1,u2,u3=symbols('x u1 u2 u3'); y=Matrix([1,x,x**2]); M=Matrix.hstack(y,y.diff(x),Matrix([u1,u2,u3])); simplify(M.det()-(u3-2*x*u2+x**2*u1))
checkable.asserts: For y'''=0 with y=(1,x,x^2) the determinant equals u1*x**2-2*u2*x+u3 (result 0). So x = (u2 ± sqrt(u2**2-u1*u3))/u1: two tangents from u to the conic.

Under y -> A y the equation becomes the original one in A^{-1}u, so x(u) is invariant under u -> A u for monodromy A (result 0).
Counterexample to the naive product trick: (X,Y) -> (cX, Y/c) fixes the product X*Y but neither factor.
